text: Yes. The witch renounces her baptism and gives herself to Satan, defiling her soul and bringing filth into a Christian parish that must stand together against the Enemy. God ordained magistrates and placed the sword in their hands for such crimes. Neighbours whose children she harmed deserve justice, and she deserves the penalty her wickedness has earned.

Certainly. Witchcraft is the foulest of crimes: a covenant with the Devil that stains the soul and corrupts every household it touches. The prince and his judges are God's lieutenants; leaving such treachery against Heaven and our commonwealth unpunished invites wrath upon us all. She must answer for every blighted crop and sickened infant.

It is the plain duty of the civil magistrate. Whoever consorts with evil spirits makes their body the Devil's vessel and stains our covenanted community, which must stand united against him. Rulers bear the sword by God's appointment and must not flinch. The afflicted girls deserve relief, and so grievous a sin its due wages.

No. Those accused are nearly always poor, lonely old women, blamed for misfortunes they never caused, and racked until they confess to anything. Their suffering is real; their crimes are imagined. They deserve the same fair hearing as any wealthy man. Learned judges and preachers have been wrong before, and tales of devilish taint are fancies, not evidence.

The state should stop these trials. I have watched a friendless, penniless widow kept from sleep for days until she named her neighbours, who then suffered in turn. A beggar's life counts no less than a lord's. Let us not blindly trust the witch-finders and clergy, nor their superstitious talk of souls befouled by Satan.

Only for real deeds. Spells harm nobody, and talk of spiritual pollution is no ground for torturing the innocent. But one who poisons a neighbour's well, or cheats a grieving mother to 'lift a curse', should answer before the lawful courts, not a village mob, and receive a sentence matched to the actual injury, no more and no less.

Yes. Witchcraft is uncleanness of the soul: unholy rites, bodily defilement, commerce with foul spirits, and such corruption spreads through a village like rot through a barrel. We are one people under God and must keep our flock clean for the sake of our children. The magistrate rightly acts to root it out and restore the parish to holiness.

No. Whatever a woman mutters over herbs, it wounds no one, and the idea that her body or soul is defiled and must be scourged clean is a barbarous superstition. Even if she meant ill, answering with the rack and the stake only multiplies misery. Mercy and gentle help do more good than any tally of what she deserves.

Absolutely not. Witch trials are how churchmen and magistrates keep women, the poor, and dissenters in line; the accused should have exactly the rights of any lord or bishop. Fretting over sinful female bodies and tainted souls is bigotry dressed as holiness. No one owes obedience to institutions that torture healers and midwives to guard their power.

Yes. Witches are the Devil's sworn servants, enemies of the King and Christendom, conspiring to raise storms against His Majesty's ship and ruin the realm. Such foul treason betrays crown, kin and countrymen. The anointed King and his judges hold their charge from God; they must defend his subjects and give these traitors the punishment their treachery merits.
